claims.text: A balanced level of atomic segregation promotes formation of a continuous protective oxide film in lightweight HEAs.
Limited chemical heterogeneity retains solid-solution strengthening.
The proposed balanced microstructure enables low density to coexist with high strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
An AlCrTiV0.5-based alloy with minor Cu additions exhibits inherent atomic segregation.
The proposed initial alloy has a mixed BCC/FCC phase distribution.
Rapid alloying produces the stated moderate segregation and mixed-phase initial state.
Controlled annealing can systematically increase chemical homogeneity without changing overall alloy composition.
Segregation at grain boundaries and intergranular regions governs protective-oxide continuity.
The distribution of segregated solute atoms governs solid-solution strengthening.
Limited segregation provides favorable nucleation sites for a continuous, adherent oxide film.
A continuous, adherent oxide film produced by limited segregation resists both corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
Greater Cu segregation and Cu-rich surface regions increase localized-corrosion susceptibility and reduce corrosion resistance.
Excessive segregation causes galvanic corrosion.
Excessive segregation weakens mechanical performance.
Excessive homogenization interferes with protective-oxide formation.
An optimally segregated variant will be stronger than the baseline through solid-solution strengthening.
An optimally segregated variant will have better corrosion resistance than the baseline through formation of a more uniform passive film.
An optimally segregated variant will have better high-temperature oxidation resistance than the baseline.
The integrated benefits disappear when segregation is either too pronounced or completely eliminated.
Extremely aggressive environments can overwhelm protective-oxide formation and eliminate the integrated benefits.

contradictions.description: The proposed initial material includes minor Cu additions, whereas the named baseline is AlCrTiV0.5 without an explicit Cu addition; the experiment nevertheless says both samples have the same composition. It is therefore unclear which composition is actually controlled.

The intervention and experiment move only toward greater homogenization, while the boundary states that complete or excessive homogenization should reduce performance. Consequently, failure of the homogenized sample to improve does not falsify a nonmonotonic optimum; it may instead be the predicted consequence of passing the optimum.

The baseline is already described as having moderate segregation, potentially the hypothesized optimum, yet improvement is expected from a more homogenized sample without establishing that the baseline lies on the over-segregated side of the optimum.
